props.title: Rustlers' Rhapsody

sections.content: **Rustlers' Rhapsody** (1985) brilliantly deconstructs Western movie tropes two years before **Mel Brooks' Blazing Saddles** (1974) became the definitive Western parody. Tom Berenger plays Rex O'Herlihan, the "singing cowboy" who's hyper-aware he's living in a formulaic Western, complete with predictable showdowns and squeaky-clean heroics. The film cleverly predates the meta-commentary style later seen in **Scream** (1996) and **Cabin in the Woods** (2012), with its protagonist actively discussing the "rules" of his genre.

sections.content: The singing cowboy genre that **Rustlers' Rhapsody** (1985) satirizes peaked in the 1940s with Gene Autry and Roy Rogers films. These squeaky-clean heroes never drank, always shot the gun out of the bad guy's hand, and randomly burst into song while riding the range. Director Hugh Wilson cleverly updates this format by having Rex maintain his naive worldview while confronting increasingly modern situations and characters who don't play by the traditional Western rules.

The film's meta-awareness creates a fascinating bridge between classic Western parodies like **Son of Paleface** (1952) and modern deconstructions like **Django Unchained** (2012). Where earlier spoofs played strictly for laughs, **Rustlers' Rhapsody** (1985) adds a layer of commentary about genre conventions themselves, questioning why Western heroes behave in such predictable ways while still celebrating the tropes that made these films beloved. sections.content: The film sits at an interesting crossroads between traditional Western comedies like **The Shakiest Gun in the West** (1968) and more pointed genre deconstructions like **Wild Wild West** (1999). Its self-referential humor laid groundwork for later meta-Westerns like **Shanghai Noon** (2000), where Jackie Chan's character similarly plays with audience expectations of both Western and martial arts film conventions.
